questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the constant factor in an exponential growth pattern
questions.stem: Ticket #4412 asks how a service archive grew from 20 GB to 320 GB over four equal quarterly periods. Which description fits the reported data?

options.text: Each quarter multiplied the stored amount by the same fixed factor of two.
Each quarter added 75 GB, so the archive grew linearly across the four quarters.
options.misconception: confuses exponential growth with a constant additive rise

options.text: The archive gained 300 GB in total, which averages 75 GB of growth per quarter.
options.misconception: believes a total increase implies a constant percentage

options.text: The archive grew at a steady 5 percent per quarter for the whole four-quarter span.
options.misconception: guesses a small fixed rate instead of computing the factor

questions.explanation: Doubling each quarter gives 20, 40, 80, 160 and 320 GB, which matches the reported total. A constant quarterly addition would describe linear growth, not this sixteenfold jump.
questions.hint: Compare the ratio between consecutive reported totals.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an exponential model at a given time
questions.stem: Ticket #4413 says a service user count follows N(t) = 400 times 1.25 to the power t, with t in years. How many users are expected after 3 years?
questions.explanation: One and a quarter cubed is 1.953125, and multiplying that by 400 gives 781.25 users. Squaring twice gives 1.5625 and then 1.953125, which confirms the same value from the other direction.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a logarithm solves an exponential equation
questions.stem: Ticket #4414 asks why solving 5 to the power x equals 125 requires a logarithm at all. Which reasoning is soundest?

options.text: Because logarithms run every exponential calculation and always give an exact integer.
options.misconception: believes logarithms always return whole numbers

options.text: Because a logarithm is precisely the exponent that turns 5 into 125.
Because 125 must be rewritten as a power of 5 before any arithmetic can begin.
options.misconception: believes a power must be rewritten before evaluation

options.text: Because subtraction removes the exponent and leaves a value that can then be added to 5.
options.misconception: confuses logarithms with subtraction on the base

questions.explanation: Since 5 cubed is 125, the exponent needed is 3, and the logarithm of 125 in base 5 returns exactly that 3. No rewriting of 125 is required, and logarithms do not automatically produce whole numbers.
questions.hint: Ask what exponent produces the given value.

5333.33 signups, because the factor 0.75 must be divided into 4000.
options.misconception: inverts the multiplication instead of multiplying

options.text: Q(t) = 1200 times 0.25 to the power t, which halves only once an hour.

options.text: Q(t) = 1200 times 0.99 to the power t, which decays by 99 percent each half hour.
options.misconception: confuses a 99 percent decay factor with a halving

options.text: Q(t) = 1200 times 0.5 to the power 2t, which halves once every 30 minutes.

questions.explanation: A half-life model raises 0.5 to the number of half-lives elapsed, so 30 minutes means an exponent of 2t. Subtracting a fixed amount cannot halve the queue each period.

options.text: Because the log of 32 plus the log of 8 equals the log of 40 and both round to 1.7.
options.misconception: adds the arguments and then approximates the result

options.text: Because the log of a product equals the sum of the logs, and 32 times 8 is 256.
Because the quotient rule turns the sum of two logarithms into one logarithm.
options.misconception: invokes the quotient rule to justify a product identity

questions.explanation: The product rule states that the log of 32 plus the log of 8 equals the log of 256, since 32 times 8 is 256. The sum rule does not apply here because the arguments are multiplied, not added.

options.misconception: confuses the two function families

questions.learningObjective: Combine two logarithms using the product rule
questions.stem: Ticket #4447 combines the log base 3 of 9 and the log base 3 of 27 into a single logarithm. What is the argument of that combined logarithm?
questions.explanation: The product rule says the sum equals the log of the product, and 9 times 27 equals 243. So the combined logarithm is the log base 3 of 243, whose argument is 243.
questions.hint: Multiply the two arguments together.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of decreasing an exponent
questions.stem: Ticket #4448 asks what happens to the value of 2 to the power x when x decreases by 3.

options.text: It triples, because each step down divides the value by three.
options.misconception: confuses the step size with the size of the growth factor

options.text: It doubles, because each step down multiplies the value by two.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the exponent change

options.text: It is divided by 8, because 2 to the power 3 equals 8.
It is divided by 6, because the exponent drops by three units.
options.misconception: adds the exponent values instead of using the base

questions.explanation: Lowering the exponent by 3 divides the value by 2 cubed, which is 8, since 2 to the power 3 equals 8. The factor comes from the base itself, not from the size of the exponent change.
questions.hint: Rewrite the change as a fraction of the base.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a transfer rate in growing units
questions.stem: Ticket #4449 says a backup copied 120 GB of a growing volume in 5 minutes. How many GB per minute did the copy move?
questions.explanation: Dividing the total volume by the elapsed time gives 120 divided by 5, which is 24 GB per minute. Multiplying that rate back by 5 minutes returns 120 GB, confirming the units.
questions.hint: Divide total gigabytes by total minutes.

questions.learningObjective: Choose between a log model and a linear model
questions.stem: Ticket #4450 compares a log model and a linear model for monthly signups. Which statement is best supported by the data?

options.text: The linear model fits better because signup growth always increases by a constant amount.
options.misconception: assumes constant absolute growth without checking ratios

options.text: The log model fits better because signups grow by a percentage that shrinks over time.
options.misconception: describes a shrinking percentage growth rate

options.text: The log model fits better because the signups eventually stop increasing entirely.
options.misconception: misreads logarithmic growth as growth that must stop

options.text: The log model fits better because the signup ratio between months stays roughly constant.

questions.explanation: A constant ratio between successive months means the log of signups grows linearly, which is what the log model captures. Log growth slows but never stops.
questions.hint: Check whether the ratio between months is steady.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a logarithm of a power
questions.stem: Ticket #4451 asks for the log base 4 of 1024 cubed, which appears inside a scoring expression. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Since 1024 equals 4 to the power 5, raising 1024 to the third power gives 4 to the power 15. The logarithm of that is exactly 15, so the cube simply multiplies the original logarithm.
questions.hint: Notice that 1024 is a power of four.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Reject an invalid logarithm identity
questions.stem: Ticket #4452 asks a reviewer to judge the claim that the log of x plus the log of y always equals the log of x plus y.

options.text: The claim is valid, because logarithms distribute over addition in both directions.
options.misconception: believes the sum rule works in the reverse direction

options.text: The claim is invalid, because logarithms have no rules for combining two terms.
options.misconception: denies every logarithm rule rather than the one at issue

options.text: The claim is invalid, because logs combine sums of arguments, not sums of logarithms.
The claim is valid whenever x and y are both greater than one.
options.misconception: invents a restriction that does not fix the error

questions.explanation: Logarithms combine a sum of logarithms into the log of a product, not the log of a sum, so the claim reverses the rule. The correct identity in this case would use the log of x times y.
questions.hint: Recall whether the rule handles sums or products.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage increase to a balance
questions.stem: Ticket #4453 says an account balance of 6400 grows by 25 percent in the first quarter. What is the balance after that quarter?
questions.explanation: A 25 percent increase means multiplying by 1.25, and 6400 times 1.25 equals 8000. Adding 25 percent of 6400, which is 1600, gives the same 8000 as an independent check.
questions.hint: Convert the percentage to the multiplier 1.25.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Define the general exponential model
questions.stem: Ticket #4454 asks a new teammate to define the exponential function that models compound interest.

options.text: A function of the form A times b to the power t, where b is the growth factor per period.
A function of the form A plus b times t, where b is a fixed amount added per period.
options.misconception: describes a linear model and calls it exponential

options.text: A function of the form A times t times b, where b scales linearly with the exponent.
options.misconception: mixes the linear and exponential forms into one expression

options.text: A function of the form t times b to the power A, where A is the exponent base.
options.misconception: swaps the roles of the exponent and the growth factor

questions.explanation: The general exponential model multiplies a starting amount A by a factor b raised to the number of periods t. The additive form describes linear growth.
questions.hint: The variable belongs in the exponent position.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Count halvings between two values
questions.stem: Ticket #4455 asks how many halvings take a 4 volt signal down to 0.5 volts in a level meter.
questions.explanation: Each halving divides the value by two, and 4 divided by 8 is 0.5. Since 2 cubed is 8, the signal needs exactly three halvings to reach half a volt.
questions.hint: Divide the starting value by the target value.

options.text: Installs rose by a constant 150 each release, so the growth is linear.
options.misconception: reads equal differences as the whole story

options.text: Installs rose by 150 percent then by 150 percent, so the growth is linear.
options.misconception: calls a rising percentage growth pattern linear

options.text: Installs grew by a constant amount of 250, which indicates exponential growth.
options.misconception: treats a growing amount as evidence of exponential growth

options.text: Installs multiplied by 2.5 each release, so the growth is exponential.

questions.explanation: Each release multiplies the previous count by 2.5, from 100 to 250 to 625, which is a constant ratio and therefore exponential growth. The added amounts rise, so the differences are not constant.
questions.hint: Divide each count by the count before it.

questions.learningObjective: Compare doubling with a fixed yearly increase
questions.stem: Ticket #4458 asks a reviewer to judge a claim that a doubling-every-year series grows faster than a series growing by 5000 units each year.

options.text: The claim is true, because doubling always adds more units in later years than 5000.
options.misconception: confuses the eventual crossover with the early behaviour

options.text: The claim is true for large enough starting values, since doubling grows faster eventually.
The claim is false, because doubling adds fewer units than 5000 in the first years.
options.misconception: rejects the claim using only the first few years

options.text: The claim is false, because a fixed yearly increase always beats a fixed multiplier.
options.misconception: believes additive growth always dominates

questions.explanation: A doubling series eventually exceeds any fixed additive increase because the multiplier applies to a growing base. Early on the additive series can be larger, so the claim holds only in the long run.
questions.hint: Compare the growth of the base over many periods.

questions.stem: Ticket #4459 asks for the annual decay rate, as a percentage, when a metric keeps 90 percent of its value each year.
questions.explanation: Keeping 90 percent means losing 10 percent, since 100 minus 90 is 10. So the annual decay rate is 10 percent, and the amount lost each year shrinks as the metric shrinks.
questions.hint: Subtract the retained percentage from one hundred.

questions.learningObjective: Contrast exponential and logistic growth

options.text: The exponential model grows without bound, while the logistic model slows as it nears a carrying capacity.

options.misconception: believes the logistic model has no upper bound

options.text: The logistic model grows faster than the exponential one at every possible time.
options.misconception: reverses which model is faster in the long run

options.text: The exponential model slows near a limit, while the logistic model speeds up.
options.misconception: swaps the saturation behaviour of the two models

questions.explanation: An exponential model multiplies the base each period and never levels off, while a logistic model slows growth as the population nears its capacity. That flattens the logistic curve.
questions.hint: Think about what each model does near a fixed limit.

questions.explanation: Ten cubed is 1000, so the log base 10 of 1000 is exactly 3. Raising the base to 100 would halve the exponent, since 100 to the power 1.5 equals 1000 as well.
questions.hint: Find the power of ten equal to one thousand.

options.text: The claims can only be compared once a starting value and a time span are given.

options.misconception: believes additive growth overtakes multiplicative growth

options.text: The claims are identical, because both describe growth from the same baseline.
options.misconception: assumes two different rules produce the same trajectory

questions.explanation: Doubling wins or a fixed addition wins depending on the starting value and the number of periods, so neither claim follows from the rules alone. The two curves can cross.
questions.hint: Consider the starting value and the elapsed periods.

It equals 36, because the exponents 12 and 3 must be multiplied together.

options.misconception: defines halving only relative to the original value

options.text: The time for the quantity to lose half of its value during the first period.
options.misconception: limits the halving to the very first period

The number of periods after which the quantity reaches half of its start.
options.misconception: confuses half-life with a one-off halving of the start

questions.explanation: Half-life is the time for the current value to be halved, so it stays the same whether the quantity started at 1000 or at 5. The starting-value framing gives a different meaning.

options.text: The response time multiplied by a constant factor each interval, since logs turn ratios into steps.
The response time grew by a constant addition each interval, which is linear growth.

options.misconception: confuses a changing quantity with a constant one

questions.explanation: A log that rises by equal steps means the underlying quantity rose by equal ratios, so each interval multiplied by the same factor. Equal additive steps would instead appear as a curve on a log plot.
